title: Kutuzov's Council at Fili
text:
In War and Peace, after the bloody battle of Borodino in 1812, the Russian army falls back to the village of Fili, just outside Moscow. Napoleon's army is approaching. Field Marshal Kutuzov calls his generals to a council of war in the best room of a peasant's hut. The peasant's six year old granddaughter, Malasha, has been forgotten on the big stove, and she watches everything from there.

The generals argue. General Bennigsen insists that Moscow, the holy ancient capital, must be defended, and others propose plans for fighting in front of the city. Kutuzov listens, sitting heavily in a corner, his eyes half closed. In Tolstoy's account he sees the question differently: whether to risk losing the army by fighting, or to lose Moscow without a battle.

At last he speaks. He says that by the authority entrusted to him by his sovereign and his country, he orders a retreat. The generals leave quietly, as if from a funeral.

Alone that night, Kutuzov cannot sleep. He asks himself when the decision that Moscow would be abandoned was really made. Yet he also swears that the French will pay for it, and that he will make them eat horseflesh. In the novel, the retreat preserves the army, and Napoleon's capture of an empty Moscow becomes the beginning of his ruin.
lesson: A leader sometimes has to make the decision no one in the room wants, and take its weight alone. Saving what matters most may require giving up what looks most important.
location: Russia (novel set at Fili near Moscow, 1812)
source: Leo Tolstoy, War and Peace, Volume III, Part 3, Chapters 3 to 4
caveat: The council at Fili was a real event of September 1812, but Tolstoy's scene, including the child on the stove, is a novelist's dramatization.
